bullets: A good on-call rotation is designed so that waking up is rare — a pattern observed holding across three different teams, including teams using Notion and Datadog.
Alerting should be action-oriented rather than informational; a page only earns its place if it tells the responder something to do.
Error budgets work when they change behavior rather than existing as a reporting metric — the framing matters because it reveals which trade-offs a team is actually making.
Outside of Sentry-class tooling, the failure mode is harder to spot; once that visibility gap is internalized, the remaining on-call design decisions get easier.
Adopting Sentry in the incident flow makes the trade-off visible — ignoring it leads teams to rebuild the same capability from scratch a year later.
PagerDuty's incident response model assumes someone owns the page; the second-order effect of unclear ownership is the part most people miss.
Systems thinking cross-cuts every on-call decision — alerting, error budgets, and page ownership are interdependent trade-offs rather than isolated choices.
Running one idea for two weeks and then iterating beats attempting a wholesale on-call redesign — the recommended starting point for improving a rotation.
